gap.statement: The best explanation for the observed dissociations and functional autonomy between presupposition licensing and collaborative coordination is that they are implemented by genuinely separate mechanisms rather than by a single mechanism with multiple outputs or by mechanisms where one is defined in terms of the other; alternative architectures that preserve unity while accommodating the dissociation data would need to be demonstrably less explanatorily adequate.

outlines.surprise: The outline places the heaviest burden on section 5's independence claim rather than on the initial data separation in section 2, betting that opponents will grant the empirical distinction but resist the independence of mechanisms. Most common ground theorists can accept that presupposition and coordination are different phenomena while maintaining they draw on a unified resource.
outlines.commitment: This structure commits to a strong cognitive architecture claim about implementation and subsystem independence rather than settling for a merely conceptual or functional distinction; a cautious version would argue only that presupposition and coordination are theoretically distinct kinds of phenomena without claiming they arise from cognitively independent mechanisms.

outlines.title: Two Mechanisms, One Name: The Disunity of Common Ground
outlines.shape: Show that the two core uses of common ground in linguistic practice satisfy different individuation conditions and respond to different theoretical pressures, then argue this pattern indicates distinct underlying mechanisms rather than aspects of one phenomenon.

sections.heading: The Individuation Test: When Common Ground Counts as Changed
sections.establishes: What counts as a change to common ground in assertion-presupposition phenomena (adding to what can be presupposed) comes apart systematically from what counts as a change to common ground in joint action phenomena (altering what coordinates planning).
sections.refuted_by: A unified set of individuation conditions governs both cases, showing that apparent differences reflect context-sensitivity in applying a single standard.
sections.address: Stalnaker's account treats common ground as a single information state that serves both assertoric and coordinative functions, with apparent differences stemming from which aspect of the state is consulted (Stalnaker 2002, 'Common Ground', Linguistics and Philosophy).

sections.heading: Functional Independence: Different Jobs, Different Pressures
sections.establishes: The assertoric phenomenon is governed by norms of public commitment and accountability to challenge, while the coordinative phenomenon is governed by efficiency conditions on shared attention and mutual responsiveness, and these two sets of norms make conflicting demands in systematic cases.
sections.refuted_by: The norms governing what can be presupposed and what coordinates planning derive from a single underlying functional principle, with apparent conflicts resolved by priority rankings within a unified normative framework.
sections.address: Clark's collaborative model treats common ground as grounding both assertion and coordination through a single principle of joint commitment to mutual knowledge, where apparent tensions reflect degrees of groundedness rather than conflicting norms (Clark 1996, Using Language, Cambridge UP).

takes_as_given.claim: What counts as a change to common ground in assertion-presupposition phenomena (adding to what can be presupposed) comes apart systematically from what counts as a change to common ground in joint action phenomena (altering what coordinates planning).

Presupposition accommodation follows norms of what interlocutors can be held publicly answerable for, while coordination updates follow norms of what enables efficient joint activity without explicit negotiation.

sections.work: establishes functional independence, which §4 needs to argue against explanations that unify via shared implementation

sections.heading: Against Implementation Unity
sections.establishes: The assertoric and coordinative phenomena cannot both be outputs of a single computational or psychological mechanism because they require incompatible architectural features: the assertoric phenomenon requires sharp boundaries and adversarial stability, while the coordinative phenomenon requires gradient confidence and rapid mutual adjustment.
sections.refuted_by: A single mechanism with sufficient parametric flexibility can generate both sharp-boundary and gradient-confidence behavior depending on task context, making architectural differences an artifact of selective attention to outputs.
sections.address: Yalcin's dynamic semantics treats common ground as a single formally characterized context set that grounds both assertion and coordination, with behavioral differences emerging from how different speech acts query or update this unified state (Yalcin 2012, 'Bayesian Expressivism', Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society).

takes_as_given.claim: The assertoric phenomenon is governed by norms of public commitment and accountability to challenge, while the coordinative phenomenon is governed by efficiency conditions on shared attention and mutual responsiveness, and these two sets of norms make conflicting demands in systematic cases.

Public commitment tracking requires all-or-nothing membership conditions that resist quick revision, while collaborative planning requires graduated confidence that updates continuously with perceived partner states.

sections.work: establishes that unity cannot be rescued at the implementation level, which §5 needs to conclude the phenomena are genuinely distinct mechanisms

sections.heading: The Convergence Verdict
sections.establishes: Common ground is not a single phenomenon but the accidental convergence of two independently operating mechanisms: one tracking mutual public commitment (what can be presupposed in assertion) and another tracking shared mental states (what coordinates collaborative planning).
sections.refuted_by: Despite individuating differently, answering to different functional pressures, and requiring incompatible architectures, the two phenomena share a deeper unity at some level of analysis not yet considered.
sections.address: The shared assumption of both Stalnaker and Yalcin that 'common ground' picks out a single theoretical kind, where apparent heterogeneity reflects our incomplete understanding rather than genuine plurality.

outlines.load_bearing: The assertoric phenomenon is governed by norms of public commitment and accountability to challenge, while the coordinative phenomenon is governed by efficiency conditions on shared attention and mutual responsiveness, and these two sets of norms make conflicting demands in systematic cases.

gap.statement: For this inference to go through, functional differences must be the kind that necessitate rather than merely suggest architectural differences, and there must be no unexplored architectural design that could serve both functional profiles.

outlines.surprise: The outline commits to architectural disunity being demonstrable from functional conflicts alone, without detailed empirical work on underlying mechanisms. This is surprising because philosophy of mind typically treats questions about mechanism individuation as requiring significant empirical input, but here the argument is that functional analysis already decides the case.
outlines.commitment: The outline commits to treating the unity assumption as more than a harmless simplification—as a substantive error that generates explanatory failures. A cautious version would leave open that 'common ground' could still usefully name a family resemblance or a role multiply realized, but this argument denies even that: it insists on calling the convergence 'accidental,' ruling out principled connections.

outlines.title: The Accidental Unity of Common Ground
outlines.shape: Establish two independent functional profiles, show they are satisfied by different mechanisms, then demonstrate that standard common ground discourse systematically equivocates between them.

sections.heading: Two Functional Profiles
sections.establishes: Common ground discourse invokes two distinct functional profiles: one governing presupposition licensing in assertion (the Assertoric Profile) and another governing action coordination in joint activity (the Planning Profile), where the Assertoric Profile requires only that information be mutually recognized as available for presupposition while the Planning Profile requires shared representation of goals and intentions.
sections.refuted_by: The two profiles turn out to be intensionally equivalent, satisfied by the same states under all conditions.
sections.address: Stalnaker's view that common ground is constituted by mutual belief about what is mutually believed, which would unify both profiles under a single propositional attitude structure. Stalnaker (2002) explicitly argues that assertion and planning both draw on the same underlying propositional common ground.

takes_as_given.claim: Assertions can presuppose content that is not part of any speaker's plan or intention.
Joint action requires coordinated mental states beyond mere mutual recognition of propositions.

sections.work: §3 needs these distinct profiles to show they come apart empirically

sections.heading: The Empirical Dissociation
sections.establishes: The Assertoric Profile and Planning Profile are satisfied by different token states in actual cases: presupposition inheritance under embedding operates independently of whether speakers share planning states, and coordination in joint action succeeds or fails independently of what can be presupposed in assertion.
sections.refuted_by: A unified mechanism is identified that produces both profiles simultaneously, showing that apparent dissociations are merely surface differences in how the same underlying state manifests.
sections.address: Yalcin's (2018) view that common ground is a single cognitive state with multiple functional roles, where the roles cannot come apart because they are aspects of a unified informational state that both licenses presupposition and enables coordination.

sections.heading: The Burden of Unification
sections.establishes: Any theory that posits a single mechanism satisfying both the Assertoric Profile and Planning Profile must either explain why that mechanism systematically produces dissociated outputs or restrict the domain of common ground in a way that leaves one profile unaccounted for.
sections.refuted_by: A unified mechanism is articulated that generates both profiles from a single state without systematically producing dissociated outputs and without domain restriction.
sections.address: A defender of Stalnaker's or Yalcin's unified account who argues that apparent dissociations are performance errors or pragmatic effects rather than theoretical problems. This represents the standard response in the common ground literature to apparent counterexamples.

sections.refuted_by: Evidence emerges that the two mechanisms are not independent but are causally or constitutively linked such that one depends on or produces the other.

sections.heading: Why the Convergence Is Not Surprising
sections.establishes: The convergence of commitment-tracking and shared-state mechanisms on overlapping outputs is explained by independent functional pressures: assertions typically concern matters relevant to joint action, and joint actions typically require publicly acknowledged terms, so the mechanisms track correlated inputs without being unified.
sections.refuted_by: The correlation between what can be presupposed and what enables coordination is shown to be stronger than can be explained by independent functional pressures tracking correlated inputs, requiring a unified underlying mechanism.
sections.address: A critic following Williamson's (2000) Knowledge First approach who argues that coincidences in functional architecture require explanation through reduction to a common source, making the two-mechanism view unstable and demanding unification.

takes_as_given.claim: Common ground is not a single phenomenon but the accidental convergence of two independently operating mechanisms: one tracking mutual public commitment (what can be presupposed in assertion) and another tracking shared mental states (what coordinates collaborative planning).

sections.work: Needed to block the objection that the two-mechanism view makes convergence inexplicable

outlines.load_bearing: The Assertoric Profile and Planning Profile are satisfied by different token states in actual cases: presupposition inheritance under embedding operates independently of whether speakers share planning states, and coordination in joint action succeeds or fails independently of what can be presupposed in assertion.

gap.statement: The empirical dissociations established in §3 must be best explained by genuine independence of mechanisms rather than by a single mechanism with two modes of operation that happen to dissociate in performance, and the burden of unification established in §4 must make the parsimony cost of positing two mechanisms lower than the explanatory cost of maintaining one.

outlines.surprise: The outline makes the critical move at §4 rather than §3: instead of resting on dissociation cases alone, it argues that unification theories face a structural dilemma regardless of how they respond to cases. This shifts the debate from trading intuitions about examples to comparing theoretical costs.
outlines.commitment: This outline commits to defending actual, robust empirical dissociations where presupposition and coordination come apart, not merely possible or hypothetical cases. If the phenomena turn out to be less stable than claimed, the entire argument collapses at §3. Most cautious versions would rely on conceivability arguments or weaker modal claims.

sections.heading: Convergence Without Unity
sections.establishes: Common ground is not a single phenomenon but the accidental convergence of two independently operating mechanisms: one tracking mutual public commitment (what can be presupposed in assertion) and another tracking shared mental states (what coordinates collaborative planning).
sections.refuted_by: The reliable co-occurrence of the two clusters in paradigm cases requires explanation by a unified mechanism.
sections.address: Clark's view that common ground is a unified foundation for all coordination in dialogue, explained by a single grounding mechanism (Clark 1996, Using Language)

takes_as_given.claim: The presupposition-licensing cluster and the coordination-enabling cluster can each occur without the other.
When two functional clusters can each occur without the other, they are implemented by distinct mechanisms rather than being aspects of a single mechanism.
Frequent co-occurrence of outputs from distinct mechanisms does not require those mechanisms to be unified.

outlines.surprise: The architecture treats the convergence as genuinely accidental rather than seeking a deeper unifying explanation, and does so through establishing independent variability rather than through arguments about theoretical parsimony or conceptual analysis.
outlines.commitment: The outline commits to denying that the frequent co-occurrence of presupposition-licensing and coordination in ordinary conversation requires or even suggests a unified mechanism, treating what looks like systematic pairing as mere contingent alignment.

outlines.title: Common Ground as Convergence: Two Mechanisms, One Phenomenon
outlines.shape: Show that two phenomena systematically diverge where a unitary account predicts they would not, then argue the best explanation is that they are independent mechanisms whose outputs merely converge in standard cases.

sections.heading: The Unitary Conception and Its Predictions
sections.establishes: If common ground is a single phenomenon tracking a unified theoretical kind, then what can be assertorically presupposed and what enables collaborative planning coordination must always align.
sections.refuted_by: Cases exist where assertoric presupposition and collaborative planning coordination systematically come apart.
sections.address: Stalnaker's account in 'Common Ground' (2002) treats the common ground as a unified set of mutually accepted propositions that serves both conversational and coordinative functions, predicting alignment; Yalcin's 'Epistemic Modals and the Problem of Disagreement' (2019) similarly treats common ground as a single information state serving multiple functions.

takes_as_given.claim: Stalnaker and Yalcin both treat common ground as picking out a single theoretical kind with a unified functional role.

sections.heading: Systematic Divergence: Three Case Types
sections.establishes: What can be assertorically presupposed and what enables collaborative planning coordination systematically come apart in asymmetric knowledge contexts, insincere assertion contexts, and group-versus-dyad contexts.
sections.refuted_by: These apparent divergences are either eliminable by refinements to the unitary account, or are merely performance errors that do not reflect the underlying competence.
sections.address: Stalnaker's 'Context and Content' (1999) treats apparent divergences as performance phenomena that do not threaten the underlying information state; Michael Tomasello's 'Origins of Human Communication' (2008) treats shared intentionality as a unified mechanism where apparent divergences reflect processing limitations rather than distinct systems.

takes_as_given.claim: If common ground is a single phenomenon tracking a unified theoretical kind, then what can be assertorically presupposed and what enables collaborative planning coordination must always align.
In asymmetric knowledge contexts, speakers can assertorically presuppose p while collaborative planning proceeds as if not-p, and this pattern is systematic across linguistic communities.
In insincere assertion contexts, what is added to assertoric common ground does not become available for collaborative planning coordination, and this dissociation is reliably produced.
Group settings permit assertoric presupposition of p while dyadic subsets of the same group cannot use p for planning coordination, showing the phenomena track different granularities of sociality.

sections.heading: The Architectural Explanation
sections.establishes: The best explanation for why assertoric presupposition and collaborative planning coordination systematically diverge is that they are outputs of two independently operating mechanisms—a public commitment tracking system and a shared mental state tracking system—whose outputs converge in standard cases but can dissociate.
sections.refuted_by: The divergence patterns can be explained by a single mechanism with context-sensitive parameters, or by performance limitations on access to a unified common ground state.
sections.address: Stalnaker's 'On the Representation of Context' (2014) argues that apparent functional dissociations reflect different ways of accessing a single underlying context set rather than distinct mechanisms; Stephen Butterfill's 'Joint Action and Development' (2012) argues that apparent dissociations in planning coordination reflect maturational limitations on accessing shared commitments rather than separate systems.

takes_as_given.claim: What can be assertorically presupposed and what enables collaborative planning coordination systematically come apart in asymmetric knowledge contexts, insincere assertion contexts, and group-versus-dyad contexts.

When two functional capacities systematically dissociate across multiple dimensions while converging in standard cases, independent mechanisms whose outputs normally align is a better explanation than a single mechanism with performance limitations.

Public commitment tracking requires only monitoring of assertoric behavior and social accountability norms, while shared mental state tracking requires mindreading and representation of others' epistemic states, giving them different computational profiles.

sections.address: Stalnaker's 'Common Ground' (2002) explicitly defends a single mechanism account where the common ground is a single information state that serves both functions; Craige Roberts's 'Information Structure' (2012) treats common ground as a unified component of discourse context that simultaneously licenses presupposition and enables coordination.

takes_as_given.claim: The best explanation for why assertoric presupposition and collaborative planning coordination systematically diverge is that they are outputs of two independently operating mechanisms—a public commitment tracking system and a shared mental state tracking system—whose outputs converge in standard cases but can dissociate.

When two mechanisms with independent computational architectures happen to produce aligned outputs in ecologically common situations, this constitutes accidental convergence rather than a unified phenomenon.

outlines.load_bearing: The best explanation for why assertoric presupposition and collaborative planning coordination systematically diverge is that they are outputs of two independently operating mechanisms—a public commitment tracking system and a shared mental state tracking system—whose outputs converge in standard cases but can dissociate.

gap.statement: The inference from systematic divergence to independent mechanisms requires that no plausible unified architecture could generate the divergence patterns—specifically, it requires that context-sensitivity, processing limitations, and selective access cannot explain why the same underlying state would license assertoric presupposition in exactly those cases where it fails to enable planning coordination.

outlines.surprise: The outline's architecture commits to showing systematic divergence before explaining it, making the paper vulnerable at section 3: if those cases are eliminable or reanalyzable, everything downstream fails. Most papers arguing for dual mechanisms hedge by presenting the mechanisms first, making the empirical claims defeasible.
outlines.commitment: This outline commits to the claim that convergence between two mechanisms counts as accidental even when it is ecologically ubiquitous and evolutionarily stable—a much stronger claim than merely saying the mechanisms are distinct, and one that invites the objection that ubiquitous, stable convergence is precisely what we should call a unified phenomenon.

free.outlines: Outline 4 uses mutual independence plus general principle; outline 5 uses systematic divergence plus inference to best explanation; outline 2 uses differential patterns; outline 1 uses architectural incompatibility; outline 0 uses cognitive evidence

divergence.sharpest: Whether the argument proceeds primarily through showing that each phenomenon CAN occur without the other (outlines 4, 5) versus showing that they REQUIRE incompatible features (outline 1) versus showing they exhibit DIFFERENT patterns of sensitivity and repair (outlines 2, 3) versus showing they are IMPLEMENTED by distinct cognitive subsystems (outline 0). This determines whether the paper is fundamentally about possibility (dissociation cases), necessity (architectural requirements), behavioral patterns (differential responses), or cognitive architecture (implementation). The choice shapes what counts as decisive evidence and what objections must be addressed.
divergence.absent: None of the outlines addresses how the two-mechanism view handles intermediate or borderline cases where it's unclear whether we're dealing with assertion or planning, or what happens in contexts where the mechanisms might conflict rather than merely dissociate. Also absent: consideration of developmental or evolutionary questions about why these two mechanisms exist or how they arose.

addresses.text: A critic following Williamson's (2000) Knowledge First approach who argues that coincidences in functional architecture require explanation through reduction to a common source, making the two-mechanism view unstable and demanding unification.

A defender of Stalnaker's or Yalcin's unified account who argues that apparent dissociations are performance errors or pragmatic effects rather than theoretical problems. This represents the standard response in the common ground literature to apparent counterexamples.

Both Stalnaker ('Common Ground', 2002) and Yalcin ('Epistemic Modals', 2007) treat common ground as picking out a single theoretical kind—they disagree about whether it is fundamentally doxastic or fundamentally dialectical, but both assume there is one thing there to be characterized rather than two mechanisms whose outputs happen to align

Bratman's account in 'Shared Agency' (2014) grounds joint action in shared intentions understood as interlocking individual psychological states, but Clark's work on 'joint activities' and Tomasello's work on 'shared intentionality' in collaborative contexts can be read as showing that public behavioral coordination rather than private mental state tracking is what does the regulative work

Clark's collaborative model treats common ground as grounding both assertion and coordination through a single principle of joint commitment to mutual knowledge, where apparent tensions reflect degrees of groundedness rather than conflicting norms (Clark 1996, Using Language, Cambridge UP).
Clark's view that common ground is a unified foundation for all coordination in dialogue, explained by a single grounding mechanism (Clark 1996, Using Language)
Functionalist accounts that allow single mechanisms to produce separable effects, as defended by Polger and Shapiro (2016, The Multiple Realization Book)

Gilbert's (1989) view that joint commitments are the foundation of both assertion norms and collaborative planning, which would make the commitment-tracking mechanism dependent on or identical to the shared-intention mechanism rather than independent of it.
Lewis's view that coordination requires mutual knowledge established through public indicators of common knowledge (Lewis 1969, Convention)

Stalnaker's 'Common Ground' (2002) explicitly defends a single mechanism account where the common ground is a single information state that serves both functions; Craige Roberts's 'Information Structure' (2012) treats common ground as a unified component of discourse context that simultaneously licenses presupposition and enables coordination.

Stalnaker's 'Context and Content' (1999) explicitly treats the common ground as a single mechanism that serves both assertoric and coordinative functions by maintaining a unified representation of shared information, where presupposition and planning draw on the same resource rather than separate ones that happen to align

Stalnaker's 'On the Representation of Context' (2014) argues that apparent functional dissociations reflect different ways of accessing a single underlying context set rather than distinct mechanisms; Stephen Butterfill's 'Joint Action and Development' (2012) argues that apparent dissociations in planning coordination reflect maturational limitations on accessing shared commitments rather than separate systems.

Stalnaker's account treats common ground as a single information state that serves both assertoric and coordinative functions, with apparent differences stemming from which aspect of the state is consulted (Stalnaker 2002, 'Common Ground', Linguistics and Philosophy).

Von Fintel's (2008) claim that accommodation is a uniform process of common ground update that repairs any kind of common ground failure through the same mechanism of state addition

Yalcin argues in 'Epistemic Modals' (2007) that common ground must be understood as genuinely shared information states that conversational participants represent and reason about, not merely as a social scoreboard, because presupposition projection is sensitive to what speakers believe about each other's information

Yalcin's (2007) claim that the common ground is individuated by its functional role in constraining assertion, which would predict uniform sensitivity to publicity conditions across all common ground phenomena

Yalcin's (2018) view that common ground is a single cognitive state with multiple functional roles, where the roles cannot come apart because they are aspects of a unified informational state that both licenses presupposition and enables coordination.

Yalcin's dynamic semantics treats common ground as a single formally characterized context set that grounds both assertion and coordination, with behavioral differences emerging from how different speech acts query or update this unified state (Yalcin 2012, 'Bayesian Expressivism', Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society).
Yalcin's view that common ground essentially involves aligned credal states among participants (Yalcin 2018, 'Expressivism by Force')
